1	from __future__ import annotations
2	
3	import argparse
4	import json
5	import math
6	from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
7	from typing import Any
8	from urllib.parse import urlsplit
9	
10	from .errors import ChronicleFlowError, NotFoundError, ValidationError
11	from .service import ChronicleFlow
12	
13	
14	def _reject_non_finite(constant: str) -> Any:
15	    raise ValidationError(f"request body must not contain {constant}")
16	
17	
18	def _assert_finite(value: Any) -> None:
19	    if isinstance(value, float) and not math.isfinite(value):
20	        raise ValidationError("request body must not contain non-finite numbers")
21	    if isinstance(value, dict):
22	        for item in value.values():
23	            _assert_finite(item)
24	    elif isinstance(value, list):
25	        for item in value:
26	            _assert_finite(item)
27	
28	
29	class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
30	    service: ChronicleFlow
31	
32	    def log_message(self, format: str, *args: Any) -> None:
33	        return
34	
35	    def _json(self, status: int, value: Any) -> None:
36	        body = json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":")).encode() + b"\n"
37	        self.send_response(status)
38	        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
39	        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
40	        self.end_headers()
41	        self.wfile.write(body)
42	
43	    def _body(self) -> Any:
44	        content_type = self.headers.get("Content-Type", "")
45	        if content_type.split(";", 1)[0].strip().lower() != "application/json":
46	            raise ValidationError("Content-Type must be application/json")
47	        try:
48	            length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", "0"))
49	            if length < 0 or length > 1_000_000:
50	                raise ValueError
51	            parsed = json.loads(self.rfile.read(length), parse_constant=_reject_non_finite)
52	            _assert_finite(parsed)
53	            return parsed
54	        except (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError) as error:
55	            raise ValidationError("request body must be valid JSON") from error
56	
57	    def _dispatch(self) -> tuple[int, Any]:
58	        path = urlsplit(self.path).path
59	        parts = [part for part in path.split("/") if part]
60	        if self.command == "GET" and parts == ["health"]:
61	            return 200, {"status": "ok"}
62	        if self.command == "POST" and parts == ["workflows"]:
63	            return 201, self.service.create_workflow(self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
64	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "workflows" and parts[2] == "schedule" and self.command == "GET":
65	            return 200, self.service.schedule_status(parts[1])
66	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "workflows" and parts[2] == "schedule" and self.command in ("POST", "PUT"):
67	            return 200, self.service.update_schedule(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
68	        if len(parts) == 4 and parts[0] == "workflows" and parts[2] == "schedule" and parts[3] == "pause" and self.command == "POST":
69	            return 200, self.service.pause_schedule(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
70	        if len(parts) == 4 and parts[0] == "workflows" and parts[2] == "schedule" and parts[3] == "resume" and self.command == "POST":
71	            return 200, self.service.resume_schedule(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
72	        if self.command == "POST" and parts == ["executions"]:
73	            return 201, self.service.create_execution(self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
74	        if len(parts) == 2 and parts[0] == "executions" and self.command == "GET":
75	            return 200, self.service.get_execution(parts[1])
76	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "events" and self.command == "GET":
77	            return 200, {"events": self.service.events(parts[1])}
78	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "checkpoints" and self.command == "GET":
79	            return 200, self.service.checkpoints(parts[1])
80	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "deliveries" and self.command == "GET":
81	            return 200, self.service.deliveries(parts[1])
82	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "advance" and self.command == "POST":
83	            return 200, self.service.advance(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
84	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "decision" and self.command == "POST":
85	            return 200, self.service.decision(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
86	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "claim" and self.command == "POST":
87	            return 200, self.service.claim(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
88	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "heartbeat" and self.command == "POST":
89	            return 200, self.service.heartbeat(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
90	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "release" and self.command == "POST":
91	            return 200, self.service.release(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
92	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "cancel" and self.command == "POST":
93	            return 200, self.service.cancel(parts[1], self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
94	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "recover" and self.command == "POST":
95	            return 200, self.service.recover(parts[1], self._body(), self.headers.get("Idempotency-Key"))
96	        if len(parts) == 3 and parts[0] == "executions" and parts[2] == "replay" and self.command == "POST":
97	            return 200, self.service.replay(parts[1])
98	        raise NotFoundError("route was not found")
99	
100	    def _handle(self) -> None:
101	        try:
102	            status, response = self._dispatch()
103	            self._json(status, response)
104	        except ChronicleFlowError as error:
105	            self._json(error.status, {"error": {"code": error.code, "message": str(error)}})
106	        except Exception:
107	            self._json(500, {"error": {"code": "internal_error", "message": "internal server error"}})
108	
109	    do_GET = _handle
110	    do_POST = _handle
111	    do_PUT = _handle
112	
113	
114	def main() -> None:
115	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run the ChronicleFlow HTTP service")
116	    parser.add_argument("--host", default="127.0.0.1")
117	    parser.add_argument("--port", default=8080, type=int)
118	    parser.add_argument("--database", default="chronicleflow.db")
119	    arguments = parser.parse_args()
120	    Handler.service = ChronicleFlow(arguments.database)
121	    server = ThreadingHTTPServer((arguments.host, arguments.port), Handler)
122	    print(f"ChronicleFlow listening on http://{arguments.host}:{arguments.port}", flush=True)
123	    server.serve_forever()
124	
125	
126	if __name__ == "__main__":
127	    main()

1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
12	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
13	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
14	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
15	  execution;
16	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
17	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
18	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
19	  execution with reason `rejected`);
20	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
21	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
22	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
23	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
24	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
25	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
26	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
27	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
28	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
29	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
30	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
31	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
32	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
33	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
34	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
35	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
36	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
37	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
38	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
39	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
40	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
41	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
42	
43	## Requirements
44	
45	- Python 3.11 or newer
46	- no third-party runtime dependencies
47	
48	## Run the service
49	
50	```bash
51	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
52	```
53	
54	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
55	has bound the port.
56	
57	## HTTP API
58	
59	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
60	
61	### Health
62	
63	```http
64	GET /health
65	```
66	
67	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
68	
69	### Create a workflow
70	
71	```http
72	POST /workflows
73	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
74	
75	{
76	  "id": "order-flow",
77	  "nodes": [
78	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
79	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
80	  ]
81	}
82	```
83	
84	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
85	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
86	
87	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
88	
89	```json
90	{
91	  "id": "order-flow",
92	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
93	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
94	}
95	```
96	
97	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
98	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow.
99	
100	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
101	
102	```json
103	{
104	  "id": "nightly-orders",
105	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
106	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
107	}
108	```
109	
110	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
111	
112	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
113	
114	```json
115	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
116	```
117	
118	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
119	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
120	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
121	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
122	`false`.
123	
124	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
125	
126	```json
127	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
128	```
129	
130	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
131	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
132	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
133	dependencies of its successors.
134	
135	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
136	
137	```json
138	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
139	```
140	
141	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
142	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
143	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
144	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
145	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
146	`retries_exhausted`.
147	
148	A task may instead declare an approval point:
149	
150	```json
151	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
152	```
153	
154	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
155	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
156	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
157	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
158	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
159	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
160	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
161	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
162	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
163	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
164	move the task.
165	
166	### Submit an approval decision
167	
168	```http
169	POST /executions/run-1/decision
170	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
171	
172	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
173	```
174	
175	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
176	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
177	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
178	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
179	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
180	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
181	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
182	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
183	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
184	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
185	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
186	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
187	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
188	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
189	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
190	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
191	404.
192	
193	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
194	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
195	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
196	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
197	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
198	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
199	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
200	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
201	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
202	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
203	shape and event stream.
204	
205	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
206	segment:
207	
208	```json
209	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
210	```
211	
212	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
213	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
214	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
215	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the entry task plus every node
216	reachable from it through `depends_on`; the body keeps the usual DAG rules and
217	must contain the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
218	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
219	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
220	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
221	loop node instead).
222	
223	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
224	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
225	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
226	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
227	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
228	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
229	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
230	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
231	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
232	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
233	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
234	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.
235	
236	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
237	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
238	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
239	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
240	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
241	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
242	exactly.
243	
244	### Start an execution
245	
246	```http
247	POST /executions
248	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
249	
250	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
251	```
252	
253	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state.
254	
255	An execution may declare a timeout:
256	
257	```json
258	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
259	```
260	
261	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
262	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
263	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
264	a timeout never expire.
265	
266	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
267	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
268	
269	```json
270	{
271	  "id": "run-3",
272	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
273	  "input": {},
274	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
275	}
276	```
277	
278	### Inspect an execution
279	
280	```http
281	GET /executions/run-1
282	GET /executions/run-1/events
283	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
284	```
285	
286	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
287	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
288	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
289	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
290	
291	### Webhook notifications
292	
293	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
294	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
295	
296	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
297	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
298	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
299	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
300	  reason);
301	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
302	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
303	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
304	
305	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
306	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
307	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
308	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
309	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
310	
311	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
312	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
313	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
314	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
315	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
316	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
317	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
318	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
319	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
320	triggered it.
321	
322	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
323	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
324	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
325	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
326	results as before.
327	
328	### Inspect the delivery history
329	
330	```http
331	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
332	```
333	
334	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
335	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
336	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
337	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
338	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
339	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
340	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
341	
342	### Schedules
343	
344	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
345	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
346	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
347	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
348	
349	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
350	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
351	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
352	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
353	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
354	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
355	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
356	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
357	
358	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
359	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
360	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
361	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
362	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
363	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
364	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
365	created is exposed through the status query below.
366	
367	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
368	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
369	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
370	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
371	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
372	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
373	
374	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
375	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
376	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
377	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
378	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
379	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
380	
381	### Declare or replace a schedule
382	
383	```http
384	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
385	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
386	
387	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
388	```
389	
390	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
391	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
392	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
393	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
394	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
395	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
396	
397	### Inspect the schedule status
398	
399	```http
400	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
401	```
402	
403	Returns the declared plan as given (`interval_seconds` or `cron`, the
404	`input`, and the `missed_policy`), whether the schedule is currently
405	`paused`, the `last_triggered_at` time, and the `last_execution_id` of the
406	most recently created execution (both `null` until the first trigger). A
407	workflow that never declared a schedule returns the definite empty result
408	`{"schedule":null}`, and a missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
409	
410	### Pause and resume a schedule
411	
412	```http
413	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
414	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
415	
416	{}
417	```
418	
419	```http
420	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
421	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
422	
423	{}
424	```
425	
426	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
427	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
428	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
429	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
430	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
431	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
432	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
433	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
434	
435	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
436	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
437	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
438	
439	### Checkpoints
440	
441	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
442	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
443	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
444	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
445	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
446	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
447	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
448	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
449	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
450	duplicating any node output.
451	
452	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
453	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
454	same state shape and event stream as before.
455	
456	### Complete the next ready node
457	
458	```http
459	POST /executions/run-1/advance
460	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
461	
462	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
463	```
464	
465	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
466	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
467	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
468	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
469	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
470	the status becomes `completed`.
471	
472	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
473	
474	```http
475	POST /executions/run-1/advance
476	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
477	
478	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
479	```
480	
481	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
482	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
483	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
484	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
485	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
486	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
487	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
488	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
489	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
490	
491	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
492	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
493	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
494	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
495	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
496	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
497	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
498	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
499	the execution stream.
500	
501	### Cancel an execution
502	
503	```http
504	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
505	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
506	```
507	
508	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
509	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
510	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
511	
512	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
513	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
514	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
515	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
516	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
517	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
518	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
519	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
520	
521	### Claim a work item
522	
523	```http
524	POST /executions/run-1/claim
525	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
526	
527	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
528	```
529	
530	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
531	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
532	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
533	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
534	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
535	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
536	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
537	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
538	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
539	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
540	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
541	
542	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
543	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
544	
545	```http
546	POST /executions/run-1/advance
547	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
548	
549	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
550	```
551	
552	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
553	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
554	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
555	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
556	an execution without any claim.
557	
558	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
559	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
560	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
561	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
562	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
563	
564	### Renew a lease
565	
566	```http
567	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
568	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
569	
570	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
571	```
572	
573	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
574	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
575	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
576	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
577	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
578	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
579	
580	### Release a work item
581	
582	```http
583	POST /executions/run-1/release
584	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
585	
586	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
587	```
588	
589	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
590	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
591	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
592	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
593	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
594	`not_found`.
595	
596	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
597	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
598	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
599	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
600	restarts.
601	
602	### Recover from a checkpoint
603	
604	```http
605	POST /executions/run-1/recover
606	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
607	
608	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
609	```
610	
611	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
612	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
613	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
614	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
615	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
616	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
617	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
618	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
619	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
620	execution state and events.
621	
622	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
623	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
624	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
625	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
626	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
627	stays consistent with the materialized state.
628	
629	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
630	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
631	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
632	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
633	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
634	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
635	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
636	
637	### Replay
638	
639	```http
640	POST /executions/run-1/replay
641	```
642	
643	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
644	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
645	and the rebuilt execution.
646	
647	## Errors
648	
649	Errors use this shape:
650	
651	```json
652	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
653	```
654	
655	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
656	return 409. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
657	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
658	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
659	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
660	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
661	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
662	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
663	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
664	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
665	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
666	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, or reusing an idempotency key
667	across different operations, is a conflict. A decision by an approver who is
668	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
669	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
670	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
671	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
672	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
673	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
674	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
675	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
676	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
677	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
678	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
679	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
680	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
681	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
682	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
683	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
684	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
685	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
686	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
687	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
688	
689	## Tests
690	
691	```bash
692	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
693	```
694	
695

# ChronicleFlow

ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.

The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:

- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
  `loop` nodes;
- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
  execution;
- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
  execution with reason `rejected`);
- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
  latest checkpoint after a restart;
- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.

## Requirements

- Python 3.11 or newer
- no third-party runtime dependencies

## Run the service

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
```

The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
has bound the port.

## HTTP API

All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.

### Health

```http
GET /health
```

Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

### Create a workflow

```http
POST /workflows
Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1

{
  "id": "order-flow",
  "nodes": [
    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
  ]
}
```

Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.

A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:

```json
{
  "id": "order-flow",
  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
}
```

See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow.

A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:

```json
{
  "id": "nightly-orders",
  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
}
```

See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.

Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:

```json
{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
```

`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
`false`.

A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:

```json
{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
```

`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
dependencies of its successors.

A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:

```json
{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
```

`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
`retries_exhausted`.

A task may instead declare an approval point:

```json
{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
```

`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
move the task.

### Submit an approval decision

```http
POST /executions/run-1/decision
Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1

{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
```

`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
404.

While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
shape and event stream.

A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
segment:

```json
{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
```

A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the entry task plus every node
reachable from it through `depends_on`; the body keeps the usual DAG rules and
must contain the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
loop node instead).

When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors.

Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
exactly.

### Start an execution

```http
POST /executions
Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1

{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
```

Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state.

An execution may declare a timeout:

```json
{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
```

`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
a timeout never expire.

An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
addition to the ones its workflow declares:

```json
{
  "id": "run-3",
  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
  "input": {},
  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
}
```

### Inspect an execution

```http
GET /executions/run-1
GET /executions/run-1/events
GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
```

The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
`state` summary, and `created_at`.

### Webhook notifications

Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:

- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
  reason);
- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.

Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.

When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
triggered it.

Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
results as before.

### Inspect the delivery history

```http
GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
```

Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.

### Schedules

A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:

- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.

Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
created is exposed through the status query below.

Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.

An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.

### Declare or replace a schedule

```http
PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1

{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
```

`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.

### Inspect the schedule status

```http
GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
```

Returns the declared plan as given (`interval_seconds` or `cron`, the
`input`, and the `missed_policy`), whether the schedule is currently
`paused`, the `last_triggered_at` time, and the `last_execution_id` of the
most recently created execution (both `null` until the first trigger). A
workflow that never declared a schedule returns the definite empty result
`{"schedule":null}`, and a missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.

### Pause and resume a schedule

```http
POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1

{}
```

```http
POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1

{}
```

Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.

Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.

### Checkpoints

Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
duplicating any node output.

Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
same state shape and event stream as before.

### Complete the next ready node

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1

{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
```

The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
the status becomes `completed`.

Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2

{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
```

The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.

Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
the execution stream.

### Cancel an execution

```http
POST /executions/run-1/cancel
Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
```

A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.

Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.

### Claim a work item

```http
POST /executions/run-1/claim
Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
```

Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.

While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:

```http
POST /executions/run-1/advance
Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3

{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
an execution without any claim.

When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.

### Renew a lease

```http
POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.

### Release a work item

```http
POST /executions/run-1/release
Idempotency-Key: release-request-1

{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
```

Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
`not_found`.

Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
restarts.

### Recover from a checkpoint

```http
POST /executions/run-1/recover
Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1

{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
```

Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
execution state and events.

A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
stays consistent with the materialized state.

Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.

### Replay

```http
POST /executions/run-1/replay
```

Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
and the rebuilt execution.

## Errors

Errors use this shape:

```json
{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
```

Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
return 409. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, or reusing an idempotency key
across different operations, is a conflict. A decision by an approver who is
not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
validation error. Request bodies must not contain
non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

90	    @contextmanager
91	    def _operation(self) -> Iterator[None]:
92	        """Scope a public operation so buffered notifications drain once, after commit."""
93	        depth = getattr(self._local, "depth", 0)
94	        self._local.depth = depth + 1
95	        failed = True
96	        try:
97	            yield
98	            failed = False
99	        finally:
100	            self._local.depth = depth
101	            if depth == 0:
102	                pending = getattr(self._local, "pending", [])
103	                self._local.pending = []
104	                # A failed operation rolls its events back, so nothing is
105	                # delivered for it; a delivery problem never reaches the caller.
106	                if not failed:
107	                    for notice in pending:
108	                        try:
109	                            self._deliver_notice(notice)
110	                        except Exception:
111	                            pass

113	    def _subscriptions_for(self, execution_id: str) -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]:
114	        """Return (label, subscription) pairs for an execution, workflow first."""
115	        row = self.store.connection.execute("SELECT workflow_id FROM executions WHERE id = ?", (execution_id,)).fetchone()
116	        if not row:
117	            return []
118	        pairs: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]] = []
119	        for owner_type, owner_id in (("workflow", row["workflow_id"]), ("execution", execution_id)):
120	            rows = self.store.connection.execute(
121	                "SELECT position, document FROM subscriptions WHERE owner_type = ? AND owner_id = ? ORDER BY position",
122	                (owner_type, owner_id),
123	            ).fetchall()

128	    def _deliver_notice(self, notice: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
129	        for label, subscription in self._subscriptions_for(notice["execution_id"]):
130	            if notice["type"] not in subscription["events"]:
131	                continue
132	            # The idempotency key is deterministic per event and subscription:
133	            # retries of this delivery reuse it, other events never share it.
134	            key = f"{notice['execution_id']}:{notice['sequence']}:{label}"
135	            record = self._attempt_delivery(subscription, notice, key)
136	            with self.store.transaction() as connection:
137	                sequence_row = connection.execute(
138	                    "SELECT COALESCE(MAX(sequence), 0) + 1 AS sequence FROM deliveries WHERE execution_id = ?",
139	                    (notice["execution_id"],),
140	                ).fetchone()
141	                connection.execute(
142	                    "INSERT INTO deliveries(execution_id, sequence, document) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
143	                    (notice["execution_id"], sequence_row["sequence"], self.store.encode(record)),
144	                )

146	    def _attempt_delivery(self, subscription: dict[str, Any], notice: dict[str, Any], key: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
147	        message = {"event_type": notice["type"], "execution_id": notice["execution_id"], **notice["payload"]}
148	        body = json.dumps(message, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
149	        tries: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
150	        status = "failed"
151	        for attempt in range(1, subscription["max_attempts"] + 1):
152	            if attempt > 1:
153	                # Increasing backoff between attempts of the same delivery.
154	                time.sleep(min(0.1 * (2 ** (attempt - 2)), 1.0))
155	            request = urllib.request.Request(
156	                subscription["url"],
157	                data=body,
158	                headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "Idempotency-Key": key},
159	                method="POST",
160	            )
161	            try:
162	                with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=subscription["timeout_seconds"]) as response:
163	                    tries.append({"attempt": attempt, "status_code": response.status})
164	                status = "delivered"
165	                break
166	            except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
167	                tries.append({"attempt": attempt, "status_code": error.code})
168	            except Exception as error:
169	                reason = getattr(error, "reason", error)
170	                tries.append({"attempt": attempt, "error": str(reason)})
171	        return {
172	            "url": subscription["url"],
173	            "event_type": notice["type"],
174	            "event_sequence": notice["sequence"],
175	            "idempotency_key": key,
176	            "attempts": tries,
177	            "attempt_count": len(tries),
178	            "status": status,
179	            "occurred_at": self.store.now(),
180	        }
